text.p: Since Europe's exchange rate mechanism (ERM) limits were stretched to 15 percent following the 1993 crisis few in the markets have taken much notice of what was going on in the system.

With bands so wide, it was assumed that the grid was unlikely to run into any major trouble, but recently the Irish punt has started to explore the outlying regions of its bilateral ranges against the lira and French franc.
"We think this is just the first sign and later in 1997 you could run into much more significant and wide-ranging difficulties," said Robert Prior, European Economist at HSBC James Capel.
The punt, riding high on the back of an extremely strong pound, is currently 11.0 percent above its central French franc rate and around 10.5 percent above it central lira rate.
In recent days the punt has got to 12.4 percent above its central lira rate.

The punt's divergence to its central Ecu rate -- known as the divergence indicator -- is currently at plus 55 percent. Under ERM rules there is a "presumption of action" when the divergence indicator hits 75 percent-- signalling the need for intervention and/or a change in monetary policy.
While direct intervention would have some impact, the latter would certainly be more effective in Ireland's case. But there are problems with rates.
Sterling is riding higher on the back of a strong dollar and that situation is likely to persist, analysts said.
With sterling outside the ERM system -- it was ejected in 1992 -- the punt will remain troublesome as long as interest rates remain where they are.
But the strength of the Irish economy means that to meet the inflation criteria of the Maastricht treaty for European monetary union (EMU), interest rates must remain high.
"So long as the pound remains so strong this problem will not go away," said Paul Meggyesi, Senior Currency Economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
"With the pound outside of the ERM a conflict will persist between the punt's sterling linkage and Ireland's ERM commitments."
The Bank of Italy has been intervening of late but on mark/lira in an attempt to keep it below 1,000 per mark and close to its central mark parity of 990.
This begs the question as to whether weakness against the punt matters as much as against linchpin currencies like the French franc or mark.
The lira is close to its central parity against both these.
In fact, if Italy is trying to shadow the old narrow band limit of 2.25 percent against the mark it has succeeded.
The lira's ghost 2.25 percent limits would fall at around 968 per mark on the upper end and 1013 at the lower. Its actual 15 percent limits on the mark stand way out at 852.59 and 1149.56.
In January, as EMU convergence trades piled on, the lira did flirt with its upper 2.25 ghost limit against the mark but at its weakest point since has only got to 1005.
So it seems the punt is at present an isolated problem for the system.
"It's highly unlikely the punt's level would be of any concern to the Italians as they push towards EMU," said Joe Prendergast, foreign exchange strategist at Merrill Lynch.
"Problems against a core currency like the French franc would ring alarm bells but the punt's situation is likely to be dismissed as a domestic Irish problem."
